title: The plan: schema, grill and approval

story: Imagine Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, went straight from RH-1234 to code. Two hours later its draft PR looks perfect by its own standard: a workgroup with no projects shows a "No projects yet" card, and a test proves it. Then you type a filter that matches nothing, and the same card appears and tells you that you have no projects, which is false. You never wrote that case into the ticket, because to you it was obvious. Now the code, the tests and the PR description all have to change.
The gap was cheap to catch, if it had been caught at the right moment. Three lines that say what "done" means, read before any code was written, and you would have seen it in thirty seconds.
hook.question: How do Nova and the requester agree on what "done" means before a single line of code is written?

read.h: Done comes first, then the checks
p: Every Nova run writes a plan before it writes code, and the order of the plan is the point. It opens with the definition of done: one to five lines, in the requester's words, that say what will be true when the work is finished. Next comes the QA plan, three to five checks that a tester could run. Each check says in plain words what a user does and sees, and what a test will read to confirm it: a test ID, an ARIA role, visible text or a row count. Never a class name, because a class name can change while the screen stays right, and the screen can break while the class name stays. At least one check must be an edge case, an unusual input that often breaks things. Only after that come the files, the steps, Nova's estimate in minutes and a guess at the risk.

Why this order? A test written after the code tends to check what the code does, not what the ticket asked for. Written first, the checks are a contract: the requester agrees to them, and later every proof in the PR points back to one of them. The estimate is Nova's own guess, measured and used to post a check-in when Nova passes it. It is never a limit that stops the work. Here is the plan for RH-1234 after you asked for one change. The second line of done and the check QA-2 are your filter case.

notes.text: Done first, in the requester's words. This is what you approve.
Each check says what a user sees, not how the code works.
The edge case. A plan with no edge case is sent back before you ever see it.
Nova's guess. Passing it means a short check-in, not a stop.

p: A plan can only be as good as what Nova knows. When the readiness check from the previous lesson says ask, or when the ticket is bigger than small, Nova asks before it plans. This step is called the grill: at most five specific questions, each with Nova's own default guess, so the requester can often answer with "yes, your guess is right". The questions go into one Jira comment that mentions the requester and into the ticket's Slack thread, and the Nova state changes to Needs info.

Then the run waits, and waiting is free: no machine is running, only a timer in Temporal, the workflow engine that saves each step, so a wait can last days. The answer arrives from either place as a signal, a message to the running workflow, Nova writes a short summary of it on the ticket so the ticket stays the source of truth, and the readiness check runs again with the answer. If the same question is still open after a second round, Nova does not ask a third time; it tells the requester that the ticket itself needs editing. Nobody answering is handled the usual way: a reminder after one day, and after two the ticket is parked and given back. RH-1234 is small and clear, so it skips the grill, which is exactly the point: the step costs nothing where it does not help.

read.h: A shape the model fills, and rules only code can check
p: The plan is read by three programs: the harness, our program in the VM that runs the Claude session; the orchestrator, the service that runs the workflow; and the Slack app that shows the plan. So its shape is a zod schema in the shared package, and the planner session ends with structured output in that shape. Most rules fit in the schema itself: one to five lines of done, three to five checks, a check ID like QA-2, a risk that is low, med or high. Some rules cross fields, such as "at least one check is an edge case". zod writes those with superRefine, a function that sees the whole object and adds its own issues.

Here is the catch. The schema the model receives is JSON Schema, and superRefine has no JSON Schema form, so the model never sees that rule. The SDK checks the model's JSON against the shape, and a plan with no edge case passes that check. So the harness parses the result again with Plan.safeParse, which runs every rule, and when something fails it sends the messages back to the planner in the same session: "qa_plan: add at least one edge case check". The planner fixes its plan, and only a plan that passes reaches a person.

notes.text: A field with a default. The next section shows why that matters for the model.
superRefine sees the whole plan. Its rule exists only in code, not in the JSON Schema.
safeParse never throws. It returns the typed plan, or a list of issues.
Each issue becomes one line, such as qa_plan: add at least one edge case check. The planner gets these lines.

deeper.h: Go deeper: input mode and draft-07
p: Two options decide how the schema is converted for the planner. target: "draft-7" is needed because the SDK validates with JSON Schema draft-07 and refuses the newer draft that zod writes by default. io: "input" describes what goes into the schema rather than what comes out of it: a field with a default, such as edge_case, is optional for the model in input mode, and required in output mode, where zod has already filled in every default. So the planner's output format is built with z.toJSONSchema(Plan, { target: "draft-7", io: "input" }), and the lab prints both lists of required fields so you can see the difference.

Before the plan is posted, a separate QA agent reads only the ticket and the QA plan and either signs it or asks for changes; the next lesson is about it. Then the plan goes out as a Jira comment and a Slack message that fits on one screen: done, the checks, the files, the estimate and the risk, with a link to the full plan. Under it are three buttons, Approve, Change and Stop, built the way you saw in the lesson on Slack apps.

Only the requester's click counts; anyone else gets a message that only they can see, saying that only the requester can decide this plan. Each button carries the plan's version, so the Approve button under plan v1 cannot approve plan v2. Change opens a box for free text, the planner gets the text and posts the next version. That is what you did on RH-1234: you pressed Change once, wrote "a filter with no match should say No results, not the empty card", and approved v2. Approval is when the real cost starts: the workflow claims a full machine for the build. While the plan waits, nothing runs; you get a reminder after one day, and after three the ticket is parked and given back.

lab.title: A plan that must earn its approval
lab.goal: Write a plan schema with a rule JSON Schema cannot carry, prove the model never sees that rule, and make the harness send a weak plan back to the planner.

guess.q: The planner's structured output is checked by the SDK against the JSON Schema made from Plan. Plan has a superRefine rule: at least one QA check must be an edge case. The planner returns three checks and none is an edge case. What happens?

options.text: The SDK rejects it and asks the model again.
options.why: The SDK only knows the JSON Schema, and superRefine has no JSON Schema form. To the SDK this plan is valid.

options.text: It passes the SDK, and only the harness's own Plan.safeParse catches it.
options.why: That is why the harness parses again with zod: it runs every rule, including the ones that never reached the model.

options.text: zod refuses to convert a schema with superRefine, so the session never starts.
options.why: The conversion works; it just leaves the refinement out without a warning.

follow.say: Write the plan schema with its one cross-field rule, and acceptPlan, which turns a parse failure into a message for the planner.
Look at what the model would receive, because the difference between output mode and input mode, and the missing rule, are both easy to miss.
follow.see:
$schema: http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#
output mode requires: [ 'id', 'user_sees', 'reads', 'edge_case' ]
input mode requires:  [ 'id', 'user_sees', 'reads' ]
superRefine in JSON Schema? false

follow.say: Save Nova's first plan for RH-1234, which has no edge case and does not mention filters, and a small script that runs acceptPlan on a plan file.
follow.see:
send back to the planner:
qa_plan: add at least one edge case check

follow.say: Now plan v2, after the requester's Change: the filter case is part of done, and QA-3 is the edge case.
follow.do:
cat > plan-v2.json <<'EOF'
{
  "definition_of_done": [
    "A workgroup with no projects shows a \"No projects yet\" card in the projects table.",
    "A filter that matches nothing shows \"No results\", not the empty card."
  ],
  "qa_plan": [
    { "id": "QA-1", "user_sees": "With no projects, the table shows \"No projects yet\"", "reads": ["visible_text"] },
    { "id": "QA-2", "user_sees": "A filter with no match shows \"No results\", not the empty card", "reads": ["visible_text"] },
    { "id": "QA-3", "user_sees": "With 1,000 projects, the first page shows 25 rows", "reads": ["row_count"], "edge_case": true }
  ],
  "files": ["frontend/src/components/ProjectsTable/ProjectsTable.tsx", "frontend/src/components/ProjectsTable/EmptyCard.tsx"],
  "estimate_minutes": 70,
  "risk": "low"
}
EOF
npx tsx try.ts plan-v2.json

follow.say: See how a plan that breaks the field rules reads to the planner, because these lines are exactly what it gets back.
follow.do:
echo '{"definition_of_done":[],"qa_plan":[],"files":[],"estimate_minutes":70.5,"risk":"none"}' > bad.json
npx tsx try.ts bad.json
follow.see:
send back to the planner:
definition_of_done: Too small: expected array to have >=1 items
qa_plan: Too small: expected array to have >=3 items
estimate_minutes: Invalid input: expected int, received number

lab.build: Add the second rule from the real plan: a UI change must say how to reach each screen state. Add screen_states as an optional partialRecord from the five states (loading, empty, error, filled, bad_data) to a string, and in superRefine add an issue on screen_states when any file starts with frontend/src/ and screen_states is missing. Run npx tsx try.ts plan-v2.json: it is now sent back. Copy plan-v2.json to plan-v3.json, add screen_states with how to reach loading, empty and filled, and run try.ts on plan-v3.json until it is accepted.
checks: peek.ts shows edge_case in the output-mode list but not in the input-mode list, and says the rule is not in the JSON Schema.
try.ts plan-v1.json is sent back with qa_plan: add at least one edge case check.
try.ts plan-v2.json is accepted with 3 checks and 70 minutes before your change.
After your change, plan-v2.json is sent back with screen_states: a UI change says how to reach each screen state.
plan-v3.json, with screen_states filled in, is accepted.
lab.fix: A teammate decided the second parse was wasted work, "because the SDK already validated the structured output", and changed acceptPlan to return { plan: output as Plan }. That week Nova posted three plans with no edge case, and one requester approved a plan whose checks would pass on a broken build. Make that change, run npx tsx try.ts plan-v1.json and watch the weak plan get accepted, then put the safeParse back.
explain: Why does the definition of done come before the files and the steps in the plan?
The SDK already checks the planner's JSON. Why does the harness parse it again with zod?
Why does each Approve button carry the plan's version?
lab.done: plan-v1 is sent back, plan-v3 is accepted, and you can say which of your two rules the model will never see.

check.q: Why does Nova's plan start with the definition of done and the QA checks, before the files and steps?

options.text: So the requester agrees on what finished looks like, and every later proof can point back to it
options.why: Done and the checks are the contract. Reading them takes seconds, and a gap found there costs nothing.

options.text: Because zod checks fields in the order they are written
options.why: Field order does not change what zod checks. The order is for the person reading the plan.

options.text: So that Nova can skip the steps when the checks are simple
options.why: Every plan has steps. The order says what matters most, not what can be skipped.

check.q: The planner returned a plan with three checks and no edge case, and the SDK reported success. What should happen next?

options.text: Post it; the SDK validated the structured output
options.why: The SDK validated the JSON Schema, which cannot carry the edge-case rule. Valid JSON is not yet a valid plan.

options.text: Plan.safeParse fails, and the harness sends the issue back to the planner in the same session
options.why: Only zod runs the cross-field rule. The planner gets one clear line and fixes its plan before any person sees it.

options.text: The run stops and the ticket goes back to the requester
options.why: A missing edge case is easy for the planner to fix. Handing the ticket back would waste the requester's time.

check.q: RH-1234's plan v2 is posted. A teammate who is not the requester clicks Approve under it. What happens?

options.text: The plan is approved, because the click came from the right Slack thread
options.why: The thread is not what counts. Only the requester's decision does.

options.text: The plan is approved, but the build waits for the requester as well
options.why: There is no partial approval. The click simply does not count.

options.text: Nothing changes for the run; the teammate gets a message that only the requester can decide this plan
options.why: Only the person who handed the ticket over approves its plan, the same person who may never approve its PR.

p: The Plan schema lives in the shared package (ai-agents/shared/src/schemas.ts), because the harness, the orchestrator and the Slack app all read it; its fields are snake_case because they are the .nova/plan.json format. The real schema has more than the lab: each QA check also names its level (unit, story, e2e, api or browser only) and its proof (a video, screenshots at 760 and 1440, a transcript or test output), and each step names its model and effort. The planner runs in ai-agents/harness/src/plan.ts on a lite VM with Opus 5.5 at medium (high for fuzzy tickets), loads the plan-and-grill and codebase skills, and saves the plan on the branch and in S3. The ticket converts the schema with { io: "input" } only; add target: "draft-7" as well.

The grill is a block in ticketToPr right after the readiness check. Writing questions is an activity (an Opus 5.5 session with no VM), posting and recording answers are activities, and waiting goes through waitForPerson: a question is reminded after 1 day and parked after 2. plan-render.ts turns the plan into Jira ADF and Slack Block Kit; the Slack app handles plan_approve, plan_change and plan_stop, and the Jira comments @Nova approve, @Nova change and @Nova stop do the same. Each button's value carries the workflow ID and the plan version.

tickets.why: The Plan schema, done first, the QA plan rules and the safeParse loop.
The grill: questions before planning, with no VM while it waits.
The one-screen plan in Jira and Slack, and Approve, Change and Stop.

words.plain: One to five lines, in the requester's words, saying what is true when the ticket is finished.
Three to five checks a tester could run, each saying what a user sees and what the test reads.
An unusual input, such as 1,000 projects or an empty filter result, that often breaks things.
Nova's questions to the requester before planning, at most five, each with a default guess.
A zod rule that sees the whole object; it is not part of the JSON Schema the model receives.

review.q: From memory: the order of a Nova plan, from the top.
review.a: Definition of done (1-5 lines), the QA plan (3-5 checks with at least one edge case, and screen states for a UI change), then files and steps, the estimate (never a limit) and the risk with its reason.

review.q: A teammate says: "Let's drop the second zod parse, the SDK already validated the JSON." What do you answer?
review.a: The SDK checks only the JSON Schema, and cross-field rules written with superRefine are not in it. Without safeParse, plans with no edge case or no screen states reach the requester.

review.q: Why does the grill cost nothing for RH-1234, and what does it cost for a fuzzy ticket?
review.a: RH-1234 is small and ready, so it skips the grill. For a fuzzy ticket it costs a few questions and some waiting, but no machine runs while it waits, and it saves a plan built on guesses.

remember: Agree on done before code: the plan starts with done and the checks, code checks every rule the model cannot see, and only the requester's click approves it.
